findings.title: A dependency cycle (or a bad plan arg) escapes `resume_item` as a traceback
findings.description: The module docstring states the CLI-facing contract explicitly: "Every refusal names the fact that refused it," and `resume_item`'s own docstring says "never raises for an expected refusal." Its handler chain, however, catches only `_Stop`, `GitEnvironmentError` and `OSError`. `_resume_locked` calls `evaluate_each_source(source, params, cf_client)`, which invokes the source function; `_cf_slices_ready_to_implement` in `src/squadron/pipeline/sources.py` deliberately raises `ValueError` for a dependency cycle (and re-logs it at ERROR before re-raising), and `_plan_arg` raises `ValueError` for a plan that is not all digits. Neither is a `_Stop`, a `GitEnvironmentError`, or an `OSError`, so the exception propagates out of `resume_item`, out of `handle_item_resume` (which only catches `typer.Exit`), and out of the Typer command as an unhandled traceback rather than a `REJECTED` outcome with a named reason. The cycle path is reachable in production: a plan with a cyclic `dependencies:` frontmatter pair makes every `sq run implement-plan <plan>` fail, and `--item` then fails differently. Converting these to `_Stop(ResumeExit.REJECTED, ...)` (or adding a `ValueError` arm) would keep the documented contract true.

findings.title: `--item` is not wired into `run()`'s mutual-exclusivity guards; `--dry-run` then dies on a bare `assert`
findings.description: `check_item_flags` covers only the three flag relationships among `--item/--decision/--instructions/--resume`. Every other option in `run()` is guarded by the block at the top of the command, and `--item` was not added to any of those checks. In `src/squadron/cli/commands/run.py` the `--dry-run` block (`assert pipeline is not None  # guarded above`) executes before the new `if resume is not None and item is not None:` block, so `sq run --resume r1 --item 401 --decision retry --dry-run` passes validation, reaches that `assert`, and raises `AssertionError` — a traceback, not a usage error. The same shape applies to `--validate`, `--list` and `--status` combined with `--item`. (`--dry-run --resume` alone already had this hazard, so the fix could live either in `check_item_flags` or by adding `item` to the existing `any([...])` guards — but the newly added flag surface currently inherits a crash path that the rest of the command spends ~50 lines avoiding.)

findings.title: A git timeout in `_select_item` is reported as "not merged"
findings.description:
```python
merged = run_git(["merge-base", "--is-ancestor", branch, target], cwd=cwd)
if merged is not None and merged.returncode == 0:
```

`run_git` returns `None` when git timed out or could not run — that is exactly the condition `squadron/pipeline/git_ops.py` treats as an unknown state everywhere else (`verify_git_state` counts "git timed out or could not run" as a failure; `_rev_count` raises `GitStateUnknownError`). Here `None` falls through and is reported to the operator as `status complete but {branch} is not merged into {target}`. The outcome is fail-safe (nothing runs), but the reason is a guess presented as a fact, which violates "Never use silent fallback values" and "get the actual error message before diagnosing": the operator will go looking for an unmerged branch when the real problem is a hung git. Distinguishing `result is None` (unanswerable → HALTED/GitStateUnknownError) from `returncode == 1` (genuinely not merged) matches the convention the rest of `git_ops` follows.

findings.title: `report.json` is parsed with casts, and a missing `index`/`name` silently becomes the string `"None"`
findings.description:
`BatchReport.load` documents "any problem raises `BatchReportLoadError`" and checks `schemaVersion` deliberately. But the per-record decode goes through raw dicts:

```python
values = {attr: data.get(key) for attr, key in _JSON_KEYS.items()}
...
index=str(values["index"]),
name=str(values["name"]),
outcome=ItemOutcome(str(values["outcome"])),
```

`data.get` returns `None` for an absent key, and `str(None)` is `"None"` — so a `report.json` whose items lack `index` or `name` loads successfully and produces records keyed `"None"`, while a missing `outcome` raises and is reported as malformed. That inconsistency is exactly what `resume_item` consumes: it matches records by `r.index == request.index`, so a silently-nulled index surfaces as "no record for item 401 in …", which names the wrong cause. The module-level dict is also the only schema definition for a file boundary; the project rules ask for Pydantic (or equivalent strict validation) at file-parsing boundaries. Requiring `index`/`name` to be present and non-null (raising `BatchReportLoadError` otherwise) would make the loader's contract true.

findings.title: The whole report is rewritten after every item
findings.description: `_execute_each_step` now calls `await _write_each_report(report, runs_dir, final=False)` at the end of every iteration, and `BatchReport.write` writes both the Markdown and the JSON document (off-thread, but still two full serializations plus two `mkdir`/temp-file/replace cycles). For a 50-item batch that is ~50 rewrites of a monotonically growing document — quadratic bytes written per run. The requirement ("a batch killed outright still leaves a report of every finished item") is met with the JSON alone; writing only `report.json` per item and both files on the final write would keep the requirement and drop most of the cost.

findings.title: `accept_decision` is run-global, so it accepts every loop in the pipeline
findings.description: The key is read from run-wide `merged_params`, and `_loop_accept_decision_result` is consulted by both loop executors for every loop whose `start_iteration == 1`. "The item's revise loop" is therefore really "every loop in the run". It is harmless for today's item-resume pipelines (`implement-plan`, `slices-plan`, `tasks-plan` each contain exactly one loop), but `run_body` in `src/squadron/cli/commands/run_item.py` sets `from_step` while leaving `accept_decision` in scope for the whole pipeline, so any future multi-loop pipeline resumed with `--decision accept` would silently short-circuit loops the operator never decided about. Scoping the key to a step name (as `override_instructions` is effectively scoped by which dispatch reads it) would make the intent enforceable rather than incidental.

findings.title: `_step_mutates` has a line over the 88-character limit
findings.description:
```python
inner = cast(dict[str, object], inner_config) if isinstance(inner_config, dict) else {}
```

That line is ~102 characters, over the project's PEP 8 / 88-column rule. I could not run `ruff` here, so whether CI fails depends on whether `E501` is in the effective `extend-select`; the project rules require at least `["E", "F", "W", "I", "UP", "BLE", "ASYNC", "B"]`, which normally brings `E501` in. Worth a `ruff format` pass regardless.
